## 3.15 Extension-type registry (new in DataFusion 54)

DataFusion 54 introduced a session-level **extension-type registry** so logical types beyond the physical Arrow `DataType` set (UUID, JSON, tensors, and custom domain types) can participate in planning. The `FunctionRegistry` trait in `datafusion_expr::registry` gained extension-type-registry methods alongside the new higher-order-function methods; the registration vocabulary is the `ExtensionTypeRegistry` trait plus `ExtensionTypeRegistration` (datafusion-expr `registry.rs`), with `DFExtensionType` / `DFExtensionTypeRef` in `datafusion_common::types`, and Arrow's canonical extension types (bool8, fixed-shape tensor, JSON, opaque, UUID, variable-shape tensor, timestamp-with-offset) shipping in `arrow-schema 58.4.0` under `extension::canonical`. Metadata-aware expressions (`with_metadata`, `cast_to_type` / `try_cast_to_type`, field-aware casts) build on this substrate — see §12.27 for the function entries. The full treatment of extension types, metadata governance, and field-aware casting lives in `docs/library_ref/datafusion_schemas_rust.md` (S7).

# DataFusion Advanced — 4) Data model: Arrow, schemas, arrays, and batches

Style target follows the uploaded advanced-reference pattern. 

## 4.0 Data model stack

```text
Logical / planning layer:
  DFSchema
    ├─ Arrow SchemaRef / Schema
    ├─ per-field qualifier: catalog.schema.table / table alias / relation
    ├─ functional dependencies
    └─ column-resolution helpers

Physical / execution layer:
  RecordBatch
    ├─ Arc<Schema>
    └─ Vec<ArrayRef>
          └─ ArrayRef = Arc<dyn Array>
                ├─ Int32Array / Float64Array / StringArray / BooleanArray / ...
                ├─ null bitmap / buffers / offsets
                └─ immutable columnar values

Expression-evaluation layer:
  ColumnarValue
    ├─ Array(ArrayRef)
    └─ Scalar(ScalarValue)
```

Arrow `Schema` describes dataset structure; DataFusion `DFSchema` extends Arrow schema information with qualifiers and functional dependencies, where qualifiers are multi-part table paths such as table, schema, and catalog. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 4.1 Value case: why Arrow is DataFusion’s runtime contract

DataFusion uses Apache Arrow as its in-memory format, so query execution operates on columnar arrays rather than row structs. Arrow `RecordBatch` is the standard batch unit: equal-length columnar arrays plus a schema; each column is contiguous and optimized for vectorized operations, while the batch forms a row chunk suitable for streaming and parallel execution. RecordBatches are immutable snapshots, so transformations produce new batches rather than mutating prior ones. ([Docs.rs][2])

Operational payoff:

| Requirement                     | Arrow / DataFusion mechanism                         |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| vectorized filtering/projection | typed Arrow arrays + compute kernels                 |
| streaming execution             | `RecordBatch` chunks                                 |
| parallelism                     | immutable batches can move across tasks safely       |
| zero-/low-copy interop          | Arrow memory layout across systems                   |
| custom sources                  | emit `RecordBatch` streams                           |
| custom functions                | receive `ColumnarValue` / Arrow arrays               |
| schema safety                   | `Schema`, `Field`, `DataType`, `DFSchema` resolution |

---

## 4.2 Imports: agent-safe default

Prefer the top-level DataFusion re-export of Arrow:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::arrow::{
    array::{
        Array, ArrayRef, BooleanArray, Float64Array, Int32Array, Int64Array,
        StringArray, TimestampNanosecondArray,
    },
    datatypes::{DataType, Field, Schema, TimeUnit},
    record_batch::RecordBatch,
};
```

The top-level DataFusion crate re-exports `arrow`, `object_store`, and, when the feature is enabled, `parquet`, because those dependencies are part of DataFusion’s public API surface. ([Docs.rs][3])

Agent invariant:

```text
Use datafusion::arrow::* in DataFusion apps.
Avoid direct arrow::* imports unless versions are deliberately pinned to DataFusion's Arrow version.
```

---

## 4.3 `DataType`: logical Arrow type

`DataType` describes the type of a field/array. The enum includes primitive fixed-size types, parametric types, timestamps, decimals, dictionaries, and nested types. Examples include `DataType::Int32`, `DataType::Utf8`, `DataType::Timestamp(TimeUnit::Nanosecond, Some("UTC".into()))`, `DataType::List(...)`, `DataType::Struct(...)`, and `DataType::Dictionary(...)`. ([Docs.rs][4])

Canonical declarations:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::{DataType, Field, TimeUnit};

let i32_type = DataType::Int32;
let f64_type = DataType::Float64;
let utf8_type = DataType::Utf8;
let bool_type = DataType::Boolean;

let ts_ns_utc = DataType::Timestamp(
    TimeUnit::Nanosecond,
    Some("UTC".into()),
);

let list_i32 = DataType::List(Arc::new(Field::new_list_field(
    DataType::Int32,
    true, // item nullable
)));

let struct_type = DataType::Struct(vec![
    Field::new("x", DataType::Float64, false).into(),
    Field::new("y", DataType::Float64, false).into(),
].into());
```

Agent rules:

* `DataType` is schema metadata, not a container of values.
* Use typed arrays (`Int32Array`, `StringArray`, etc.) to hold values.
* Nested `DataType::List` / `Struct` includes child `Field` definitions, so child nullability is modeled separately from parent nullability.
* Dictionary/string equivalence is nuanced in DataFusion; `DFSchema::datatype_is_logically_equal` treats dictionary-encoded UTF8 and plain UTF8 as logically equivalent in some contexts. ([Docs.rs][5])

---

## 4.4 `Field`: one column definition

A `Field` describes a single column in a `Schema`; it contains name, data type, nullable flag, and metadata. Arrow extension types are encoded through `Field` metadata. ([Docs.rs][6])

### Scalar field syntax

```rust
use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::{DataType, Field};

let id = Field::new("id", DataType::Int64, false);
let name = Field::new("name", DataType::Utf8, true);
let active = Field::new("active", DataType::Boolean, false);
```

### Metadata syntax

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;
use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::{DataType, Field};

let mut meta = HashMap::new();
meta.insert("semantic_type".to_string(), "email".to_string());

let email = Field::new("email", DataType::Utf8, true)
    .with_metadata(meta);
```

### Nested field syntax

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::{DataType, Field};

let tags = Field::new_list(
    "tags",
    Arc::new(Field::new_list_field(DataType::Utf8, true)),
    true, // list column nullable
);

let point = Field::new_struct(
    "point",
    vec![
        Arc::new(Field::new("x", DataType::Float64, false)),
        Arc::new(Field::new("y", DataType::Float64, false)),
    ],
    false,
);
```

Arrow provides constructors such as `Field::new`, `Field::new_list_field`, `Field::new_struct`, `Field::new_list`, `Field::new_large_list`, `Field::new_fixed_size_list`, and `Field::new_map`; each encodes both type and nullability contracts for the parent/child relation. ([Docs.rs][6])

Agent nullability rule:

```text
Field::new("x", DataType::Int32, false)  => column must be non-null by schema contract.
Field::new("x", DataType::Int32, true)   => column may contain nulls.
DataType::List(FieldRef(item nullable))  => list item nullability is independent of list column nullability.
```

---

## 4.5 `Schema`: ordered columns + schema metadata

`Schema` describes metadata for an ordered sequence of relative types; it contains `fields` and schema-level key/value `metadata`. Arrow docs stress that schema metadata is not part of the physical memory layout. ([Docs.rs][7])

### Basic schema

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::{DataType, Field, Schema};

let schema = Arc::new(Schema::new(vec![
    Field::new("id", DataType::Int64, false),
    Field::new("name", DataType::Utf8, true),
    Field::new("score", DataType::Float64, true),
]));
```

### Schema metadata

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;
use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::{DataType, Field, Schema};

let mut metadata = HashMap::new();
metadata.insert("source".to_string(), "events-v2".to_string());
metadata.insert("owner".to_string(), "analytics".to_string());

let schema = Schema::new_with_metadata(
    vec![
        Field::new("event_id", DataType::Utf8, false),
        Field::new("ts", DataType::Timestamp(
            datafusion::arrow::datatypes::TimeUnit::Nanosecond,
            Some("UTC".into()),
        ), false),
    ],
    metadata,
);
```

`Schema::new` creates a schema from a sequence of `Field` values, while `Schema::new_with_metadata` also attaches key/value metadata. `Schema::project` can create a projected schema, and `Schema::try_merge` can merge compatible schemas; Arrow docs show nullability widening during merge. ([Docs.rs][7])

Agent rules:

* Use `Arc<Schema>` for `RecordBatch`, `TableProvider`, and shared schema state.
* Use schema metadata for non-execution annotations only; do not assume DataFusion optimizer semantics from arbitrary metadata.
* Use `Schema::try_merge` carefully for schema evolution; nullability and nested-field compatibility matter.
* Do not encode table qualifiers in Arrow `Schema`; use `DFSchema` for query-planning qualification.

---

## 4.6 `ArrayRef`: typed column behind dynamic dispatch

`ArrayRef` is the standard erased Arrow column handle:

```rust
type ArrayRef = Arc<dyn Array>;
```

Arrow’s tabular representation combines a `Schema` and a corresponding list of `ArrayRef` values into a `RecordBatch`. ([Docs.rs][8])

### Basic arrays

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use datafusion::arrow::array::{
    ArrayRef, BooleanArray, Float64Array, Int64Array, StringArray,
};

let ids: ArrayRef = Arc::new(Int64Array::from(vec![1, 2, 3]));
let names: ArrayRef = Arc::new(StringArray::from(vec![
    Some("alice"),
    None,
    Some("carol"),
]));
let scores: ArrayRef = Arc::new(Float64Array::from(vec![
    Some(9.5),
    Some(8.0),
    None,
]));
let active: ArrayRef = Arc::new(BooleanArray::from(vec![true, false, true]));
```

### Downcast pattern

```rust
use datafusion::arrow::array::{ArrayRef, Int64Array};

fn sum_i64(array: &ArrayRef) -> datafusion::error::Result<i64> {
    let arr = array
        .as_any()
        .downcast_ref::<Int64Array>()
        .ok_or_else(|| datafusion::error::DataFusionError::Execution(
            "expected Int64Array".to_string()
        ))?;

    let mut acc = 0i64;
    for i in 0..arr.len() {
        if !arr.is_null(i) {
            acc += arr.value(i);
        }
    }
    Ok(acc)
}
```

Agent rules:

* `ArrayRef` erases the concrete array type; downcast only after checking schema `DataType`.
* Use `as_any().downcast_ref::<T>()` in custom kernels/UDFs.
* Null handling is explicit: check `is_null(i)` or use iterator APIs returning `Option<T>`.
* Do not assume `DataType::Utf8` implies `StringArray` in every logical comparison context; DataFusion may treat `Utf8`, `Utf8View`, or dictionary-encoded strings as logically equivalent in planning contexts. ([Docs.rs][5])

---

## 4.7 `RecordBatch`: execution unit

A `RecordBatch` is a two-dimensional column-oriented dataset with a schema. It contains contiguous arrays, all arrays have the same length, and each array’s datatype must match the corresponding schema field. `RecordBatch::try_new` validates non-empty columns, matching field count, matching data types, and equal column lengths. ([Docs.rs][9])

### Safe constructor

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::arrow::{
    array::{ArrayRef, Int64Array, StringArray},
    datatypes::{DataType, Field, Schema},
    record_batch::RecordBatch,
};

let schema = Arc::new(Schema::new(vec![
    Field::new("id", DataType::Int64, false),
    Field::new("name", DataType::Utf8, true),
]));

let id: ArrayRef = Arc::new(Int64Array::from(vec![1, 2, 3]));
let name: ArrayRef = Arc::new(StringArray::from(vec![
    Some("alice"),
    None,
    Some("carol"),
]));

let batch = RecordBatch::try_new(schema, vec![id, name])?;
```

### Iterator constructor

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use datafusion::arrow::{
    array::{ArrayRef, Float32Array, Int32Array},
    record_batch::RecordBatch,
};

let batch = RecordBatch::try_from_iter([
    ("col1", Arc::new(Int32Array::from_iter([1, 2, 3])) as ArrayRef),
    ("col2", Arc::new(Float32Array::from_iter([1.0, 6.3, 4.0])) as ArrayRef),
])?;
```

Arrow’s crate docs show `RecordBatch::try_from_iter` as a convenient way to combine columns into tabular data. ([Docs.rs][8])

### DataFusion input

```rust
use datafusion::prelude::*;

let ctx = SessionContext::new();
let df = ctx.read_batch(batch)?;
df.show().await?;
```

Agent rules:

* Use `RecordBatch::try_new` in production/adapters.
* Use `RecordBatch::try_from_iter` for tests/prototypes.
* Batch length = `batch.num_rows()`.
* Column count = `batch.num_columns()`.
* Column order must match schema order.
* `RecordBatch` is immutable; transformations allocate/return new batches.
* Avoid huge batches; DataFusion execution defaults are batch-oriented and streaming-friendly.

---

## 4.8 Nullable columns and null semantics

Nullability exists at three levels:

```text
Field.nullable          => schema-level permission for nulls
Array null bitmap       => runtime null presence
ScalarValue::<T>(None)  => scalar NULL of type T
ScalarValue::Null       => untyped NULL placeholder
```

### Nullable array

```rust
use datafusion::arrow::array::Int32Array;

let a = Int32Array::from(vec![
    Some(10),
    None,
    Some(30),
]);

assert_eq!(a.len(), 3);
assert_eq!(a.null_count(), 1);
assert!(a.is_null(1));
```

### Non-null field with null array: invalid batch

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use datafusion::arrow::{
    array::{ArrayRef, Int32Array},
    datatypes::{DataType, Field, Schema},
    record_batch::RecordBatch,
};

let schema = Arc::new(Schema::new(vec![
    Field::new("x", DataType::Int32, false), // non-nullable
]));

let x: ArrayRef = Arc::new(Int32Array::from(vec![Some(1), None]));

// expect error: field says non-nullable but array has nulls
let batch = RecordBatch::try_new(schema, vec![x]);
assert!(batch.is_err());
```

`RecordBatch::try_new` validates schema/array compatibility; Arrow docs explicitly list matching data types and equal column lengths as constructor requirements. Nullability enforcement is part of Arrow’s schema/data validity contract. ([Docs.rs][9])

Agent rules:

* `nullable = true` does not mean “all values are null”; it means nulls are allowed.
* `nullable = false` is a contract; never create batches with nulls for that field.
* SQL `NULL` maps to `ScalarValue`/array nulls depending on context.
* UDFs must explicitly define null behavior; do not blindly call `.value(i)` without null checks.

---

## 4.9 `ScalarValue` vs arrays

In logical expressions, literals are `ScalarValue`s. DataFusion’s `Expr` docs show `lit(42i64)` becoming `Expr::Literal(ScalarValue::Int64(Some(42)), None)`, typed NULL as `Expr::Literal(ScalarValue::Int64(None), None)`, and untyped NULL as `lit(ScalarValue::Null)`. ([Docs.rs][10])

```rust
use datafusion::common::ScalarValue;
use datafusion::prelude::*;

let expr_i64 = lit(42i64);
let typed_null = Expr::Literal(ScalarValue::Int64(None), None);
let untyped_null = lit(ScalarValue::Null);
```

In physical expression evaluation, `ColumnarValue` represents either an array or a scalar. `ColumnarValue::Scalar` means a single value repeated logically across rows; `ColumnarValue::Array` means a column of Arrow data. This scalar representation is a performance optimization because constants do not need to be expanded into repeated arrays unless necessary. ([Docs.rs][11])

```rust
use datafusion::logical_expr::ColumnarValue;
use datafusion::common::ScalarValue;

let scalar = ColumnarValue::Scalar(ScalarValue::Int32(Some(100)));
```

### Convert scalar to array only when necessary

```rust
use datafusion::logical_expr::ColumnarValue;

fn force_array(value: ColumnarValue, rows: usize) -> datafusion::error::Result<datafusion::arrow::array::ArrayRef> {
    value.into_array(rows)
}
```

`ColumnarValue::into_array` repeats a scalar value to create an Arrow array of a given row count, but the docs warn this is less efficient than handling the scalar directly; performance-sensitive custom functions/operators should specialize scalar handling. ([Docs.rs][11])

Agent rules:

* Logical literals: `ScalarValue`.
* Runtime columns: `ArrayRef`.
* UDF inputs/outputs: usually `ColumnarValue`.
* Avoid materializing scalars into arrays in tight loops if a scalar-specialized path is possible.

---

## 4.10 `DFSchema` vs Arrow `Schema`

### Arrow `Schema`

```text
Schema
  ├─ ordered Fields
  └─ schema metadata
```

Use for physical data, Arrow IPC/Parquet/CSV/JSON IO, `RecordBatch`, `TableProvider::schema`, and runtime data validation.

### DataFusion `DFSchema`

```text
DFSchema
  ├─ inner Arrow Schema
  ├─ optional qualifier per field
  ├─ functional dependencies
  └─ logical column-resolution API
```

Use for logical planning, expression type resolution, join schemas, SQL binding, and ambiguity detection across multiple relations.

The Expr guide explicitly states that Arrow `Schema` defines column names and data types, while `DFSchema` adds qualifiers such as table names and is valuable for queries involving multiple tables. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 4.11 Creating `DFSchema`

### Unqualified from Arrow schema

```rust
use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::{DataType, Field, Schema};
use datafusion::common::{Column, DFSchema};

let arrow_schema = Schema::new(vec![
    Field::new("c1", DataType::Int32, false),
]);

let df_schema = DFSchema::try_from(arrow_schema)?;
let col = Column::new_unqualified("c1");

assert!(df_schema.has_column(&col));
```

### Qualified from Arrow schema

```rust
use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::{DataType, Field, Schema};
use datafusion::common::{Column, DFSchema};

let arrow_schema = Schema::new(vec![
    Field::new("c1", DataType::Int32, false),
]);

let df_schema = DFSchema::try_from_qualified_schema("t1", &arrow_schema)?;
let qualified = Column::from_qualified_name("t1.c1");
let unqualified = Column::from_qualified_name("c1");

assert!(df_schema.has_column(&qualified));
assert!(df_schema.has_column(&unqualified)); // allowed when unambiguous
```

The DFSchema docs show `DFSchema::try_from_qualified_schema("t1", &arrow_schema)` and note that unqualified access is also possible when unambiguous. ([Docs.rs][5])

### Convert back to Arrow schema

```rust
let arrow_schema_ref = df_schema.inner();   // Arc<Schema>
let arrow_schema = df_schema.as_arrow();    // &Schema
```

`DFSchema::as_arrow` and `inner` return the inner Arrow schema but do **not** include qualifier information. ([Docs.rs][5])

Agent rules:

* Use `DFSchema` for planning and resolving `Column`.
* Use Arrow `Schema` for actual batch construction.
* Qualifier metadata is not preserved when converting back to Arrow schema.
* Unqualified resolution is acceptable only when column name is unambiguous.
* Preserve qualifiers after joins to avoid ambiguous same-name columns.

---

## 4.12 Schema qualifiers

Qualifier examples:

```text
t.c1
schema.table.c1
catalog.schema.table.c1
alias.c1
```

In `DFSchema`, each field can have an optional `TableReference` qualifier. Methods include `qualified_field`, `field_with_name`, `qualified_field_with_name`, `fields_with_qualified`, `qualified_fields_with_unqualified_name`, `columns_with_unqualified_name`, and `columns`. These APIs support exact lookup, ambiguous-name detection, and join/schema construction. ([Docs.rs][5])

### Inspect qualifiers

```rust
for (qualifier, field) in df_schema.iter() {
    match qualifier {
        Some(q) => println!("{q}.{}: {:?}", field.name(), field.data_type()),
        None => println!("{}: {:?}", field.name(), field.data_type()),
    }
}
```

### Lookup by qualified column

```rust
use datafusion::common::Column;

let col = Column::from_qualified_name("orders.customer_id");
let index = df_schema.index_of_column(&col)?;
let (qualifier, field) = df_schema.qualified_field(index);

println!("qualifier={qualifier:?}, name={}", field.name());
```

### Ambiguity-safe lookup

```rust
let matches = df_schema.columns_with_unqualified_name("id");

if matches.len() == 1 {
    // safe
} else if matches.is_empty() {
    // unknown column
} else {
    // ambiguous column: require qualifier
}
```

Agent rules:

* After joins, never assume `col("id")` resolves to the intended side.
* Prefer qualified columns in generated plans after multi-table operations.
* Use `DFSchema` lookup methods for validation, not string heuristics.
* `DFSchema::join` errors on duplicate field names; `merge` ignores duplicate fields with specified precedence behavior. ([Docs.rs][5])

---

## 4.13 Common Rust ownership patterns

### Schema reference

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::Schema;

type SchemaRef = Arc<Schema>;
```

Use `Arc<Schema>` because schemas are shared across batches, table providers, execution plans, and streams.

### Field reference

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::Field;

type FieldRef = Arc<Field>;
```

Arrow APIs frequently use `Arc<Field>` for nested types and schema internals.

### Array reference

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use datafusion::arrow::array::{Array, ArrayRef};

let arr: ArrayRef = Arc::new(datafusion::arrow::array::Int32Array::from(vec![1, 2, 3]));
```

Use `Arc<dyn Array>` because `RecordBatch` columns are heterogeneously typed.

### Batch reference

```rust
use datafusion::arrow::record_batch::RecordBatch;

fn consume(batch: &RecordBatch) {
    let schema = batch.schema();
    let rows = batch.num_rows();
    let cols = batch.num_columns();
}
```

Agent rule:

```text
Arc<Schema>      = shared immutable schema
Arc<Field>       = shared field definition, especially nested fields
Arc<dyn Array>   = shared immutable typed column behind dynamic dispatch
RecordBatch      = schema + same-length ArrayRef columns
DFSchema         = logical schema + qualifiers
```

---

## 4.14 End-to-end: build Arrow data, query with DataFusion

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::arrow::{
    array::{ArrayRef, Float64Array, Int64Array, StringArray},
    datatypes::{DataType, Field, Schema},
    record_batch::RecordBatch,
    util::pretty::pretty_format_batches,
};
use datafusion::prelude::*;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let schema = Arc::new(Schema::new(vec![
        Field::new("customer_id", DataType::Int64, false),
        Field::new("region", DataType::Utf8, true),
        Field::new("amount", DataType::Float64, false),
    ]));

    let customer_id: ArrayRef = Arc::new(Int64Array::from(vec![1, 2, 3, 4]));
    let region: ArrayRef = Arc::new(StringArray::from(vec![
        Some("us"),
        Some("eu"),
        None,
        Some("us"),
    ]));
    let amount: ArrayRef = Arc::new(Float64Array::from(vec![10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0]));

    let batch = RecordBatch::try_new(
        schema,
        vec![customer_id, region, amount],
    )?;

    let ctx = SessionContext::new();
    let df = ctx.read_batch(batch)?;

    let result = df
        .filter(col("amount").gt(lit(15.0)))?
        .select(vec![
            col("customer_id"),
            col("region"),
            col("amount"),
        ])?
        .collect()
        .await?;

    println!("{}", pretty_format_batches(&result)?);

    Ok(())
}
```

---

## 4.15 End-to-end: DataFusion schema qualification

```rust
use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::{DataType, Field, Schema};
use datafusion::common::{Column, DFSchema};

fn main() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let orders_arrow = Schema::new(vec![
        Field::new("id", DataType::Int64, false),
        Field::new("customer_id", DataType::Int64, false),
    ]);

    let customers_arrow = Schema::new(vec![
        Field::new("id", DataType::Int64, false),
        Field::new("name", DataType::Utf8, true),
    ]);

    let orders = DFSchema::try_from_qualified_schema("orders", &orders_arrow)?;
    let customers = DFSchema::try_from_qualified_schema("customers", &customers_arrow)?;

    assert!(orders.has_column(&Column::from_qualified_name("orders.id")));
    assert!(customers.has_column(&Column::from_qualified_name("customers.id")));

    let joined = orders.join(&customers)?;

    // Ambiguous unqualified `id`: both orders.id and customers.id exist.
    let ids = joined.columns_with_unqualified_name("id");
    assert_eq!(ids.len(), 2);

    Ok(())
}
```

`DFSchema::join` creates a schema containing fields from both inputs and errors on duplicate field names; `columns_with_unqualified_name` returns all matching columns, enabling ambiguity detection. ([Docs.rs][5])

---

## 4.16 Schema equivalence and compatibility

`DFSchema` exposes multiple equivalence concepts:

| Method / concept                 | Meaning                                                                           |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `matches_arrow_schema`           | unqualified DFSchema field names match Arrow schema field names                   |
| `has_equivalent_names_and_types` | same qualified names with compatible data types; ignores nullability and metadata |
| `datatype_is_logically_equal`    | weaker logical comparison; e.g. dictionary-encoded string may equal plain string  |
| `datatype_is_semantically_equal` | semantic type comparison with broader metadata/nullability tolerance              |
| `strip_qualifiers`               | remove all qualifiers                                                             |
| `replace_qualifier`              | assign new qualifier to all fields                                                |

DFSchema docs distinguish logical equality from stricter semantic equality and explicitly cite examples such as dictionary-encoded UTF8 vs plain UTF8 and `Utf8` vs `Utf8View`. ([Docs.rs][5])

Agent rules:

* For physical `RecordBatch` construction, require exact Arrow field type compatibility.
* For logical plan rewrite validation, use DFSchema equivalence helpers.
* Do not use stringified schema output as compatibility logic.
* Avoid stripping qualifiers unless moving from planning context to output/user display context.

---

## 4.17 Working with expressions and schemas

`Expr` represents logical computations such as `A + 1`, `CAST(c1 AS int)`, literals, column references, scalar/aggregate/window functions, and more. Expression creation is usually easier through `col`, `lit`, aliases, casts, and fluent methods than by directly building enum variants. `ExprSchemable::get_type` can access an expression’s `DataType` and nullability against a schema. ([Docs.rs][10])

```rust
use datafusion::common::DFSchema;
use datafusion::logical_expr::ExprSchemable;
use datafusion::prelude::*;

fn infer_expr(df_schema: &DFSchema) -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let expr = col("amount") + lit(10.0);
    let dtype = expr.get_type(df_schema)?;
    let nullable = expr.nullable(df_schema)?;

    println!("type={dtype:?}, nullable={nullable}");
    Ok(())
}
```

Agent rules:

* `Expr` type/nullability inference requires `DFSchema`, not just Arrow `Schema`.
* Use `DFSchema` because column names may be qualified.
* Literal types are strongly typed; `lit(42i64)` differs from `lit(42i32)`.
* Untyped NULL may be coerced by optimizer/context; typed NULL is explicit.

---

## 4.18 Deployment guidance

### TableProvider / data source authors

Return stable `Arc<Schema>` from `TableProvider::schema()`. Output `RecordBatch` arrays must exactly match that schema’s field count, order, type, and nullability. Use `RecordBatch::try_new` in tests to validate provider output. Arrow `RecordBatch` constructor rules enforce field count, data type equality, and equal column lengths. ([Docs.rs][9])

### UDF authors

Handle both scalar and array inputs. `ColumnarValue::Scalar` is not a special case to ignore; it represents a logically repeated value and can be much cheaper than materializing a full array. Provide a scalar-specialized path when performance matters. ([Docs.rs][11])

### Query-generation agents

Generate qualified columns after joins. If two relations both contain `id`, unqualified `col("id")` is ambiguous. Validate against `DFSchema::columns_with_unqualified_name` or use relation-qualified `Column`s. `DFSchema` offers qualified and unqualified lookup helpers for exactly this resolution work. ([Docs.rs][5])

### API / service authors

Stream `RecordBatch` values. Do not row-materialize early unless the response format requires it. Keep Arrow batches as the boundary between DataFusion and serialization layers, especially for Arrow IPC, Parquet, Arrow Flight, or columnar internal APIs.

### Schema evolution

Use explicit schema compatibility checks at ingestion boundaries. Decide whether compatibility is physical exactness, logical equivalence, or user-facing semantic equivalence. DataFusion’s DFSchema equality helpers encode different levels of tolerance; choose deliberately. ([Docs.rs][5])

---

## 4.19 Anti-pattern inventory

* Direct `arrow::*` imports with a version not matching DataFusion.
* Building a `RecordBatch` with columns in a different order from schema fields.
* Calling `.value(i)` on arrays without checking `is_null(i)`.
* Marking `Field::new(..., nullable=false)` for data that can contain nulls.
* Stripping `DFSchema` qualifiers before resolving expressions in joins.
* Treating Arrow `Schema` as if it stores table/catalog names.
* Treating `ScalarValue` and one-row arrays as equivalent for performance-sensitive UDFs.
* Expanding scalar constants into arrays in every UDF call path.
* Snapshotting schema display strings as the only compatibility check.
* Using `RecordBatch::new_unchecked` in application code.
* Inferring output schema from first batch only when stream can be empty or schema-evolving.
* Using unqualified `col("id")` after joins with repeated field names.
* Assuming schema metadata affects DataFusion optimization unless a specific DataFusion feature consumes it.

---

## 4.20 Agent checklist

```text
[ ] Use datafusion::arrow re-exports.
[ ] Model physical data as Arc<Schema> + Vec<ArrayRef> -> RecordBatch.
[ ] Use Field::new(name, DataType, nullable) for every column.
[ ] Validate data with RecordBatch::try_new.
[ ] Treat ArrayRef as Arc<dyn Array>; downcast after schema/type check.
[ ] Handle nulls explicitly in custom logic.
[ ] Use ScalarValue for literals and ColumnarValue for physical expression outputs.
[ ] Avoid scalar-to-array expansion when a scalar-specialized path is available.
[ ] Use DFSchema for logical planning, expression inference, and column resolution.
[ ] Preserve qualifiers across multi-table plans.
[ ] Convert DFSchema to Arrow Schema only at physical/output boundaries.
[ ] Use aliases and qualified names to avoid ambiguity.
[ ] Test schema mismatch, nullability mismatch, type mismatch, and duplicate-name cases.
```
