## 21.25 Morsel-driven scans and file-stream work stealing (DataFusion 54)

DataFusion 54 rebuilt file scanning around **morsel-driven parallelism with work stealing**: instead of statically assigning each file group to one partition's stream, sibling scan partitions pull unopened files (morsels) from a shared queue, so a partition that finishes its files early steals remaining work instead of idling. Reported speedups reach roughly 2× on skewed scans (few large files among many small ones, or unbalanced file groups).

The moving parts (in `datafusion-datasource`):

* **`DataSource::open_with_args(OpenArgs)`** — new trait surface. `OpenArgs { partition, context, sibling_state }` extends the old `open(partition, context)` with optional **sibling-shared execution state** (`Option<Arc<dyn Any + Send + Sync>>`). The default implementation ignores `sibling_state` and delegates to `open`, so existing custom `DataSource` impls keep compiling — but they do not participate in work stealing until they implement `open_with_args` (and `create_sibling_state`).
* **`DataSource::create_sibling_state()`** — called once per plan execution by `DataSourceExec`; the returned state is handed to every partition's `open_with_args` call. `FileScanConfig` returns its shared work queue here.
* **`SharedWorkSource`** — the engine-internal shared queue of unopened files that sibling `FileStream`s drain cooperatively (crate-private in `datafusion_datasource::file_stream`; you interact with it only through the surfaces above).
* **`FileScanConfig.partitioned_by_file_group: bool`** (builder: `with_partitioned_by_file_group(true)`) — **disables** sharing for that scan: `create_sibling_state` returns `None` when this flag is set (or when `preserve_order` requires stable per-partition file order), and each partition then reads exactly its assigned file group.

Configuration reality check: **there is no `enable_file_stream_work_stealing` configuration key in DataFusion 54.1.0.** Work stealing is gated structurally — by whether the data source creates sibling state and whether `partitioned_by_file_group`/`preserve_order` suppress it — not by a SQL-settable option. Do not write `SET datafusion.execution.enable_file_stream_work_stealing = ...`; the key does not exist.

Distributed-execution warning: work stealing assumes all sibling partitions of a `DataSourceExec` run in the same process and can share the queue. Engines that ship individual partitions to isolated tasks (Ballista-style scheduling, or any executor that runs `execute(partition, ..)` in separate processes) **must set `partitioned_by_file_group = true`** on their scans — otherwise each isolated task constructs its own queue containing *all* files and every file is read once per task.

```text
Scan partition timeline (skewed files, stealing on):
  partition 0: [huge_file.parquet.....................]
  partition 1: [small_1][small_2][steals small_5][steals small_6]
  partition 2: [small_3][small_4][steals small_7]
```

Agent rules:

```text
Custom DataSource impls: implement open_with_args + create_sibling_state to opt into stealing.
Set partitioned_by_file_group=true whenever partition-to-file-group mapping is a correctness contract.
Set partitioned_by_file_group=true for distributed/isolated per-partition execution.
Do not reference an enable_file_stream_work_stealing config key; it does not exist in 54.1.0.
Expect scan output row interleaving to change vs 53; do not depend on file order without preserve_order.
```

# DataFusion Advanced — 22) Query optimizer

Style target follows the uploaded advanced-reference pattern. 

## 22.0 Optimizer mental model

```text id="sxtcu1"
SQL / DataFrame / LogicalPlanBuilder
  → initial LogicalPlan
      ├─ AnalyzerRule / function rewrites
      │   └─ semantic validity: type coercion, grouping resolution, function rewrites
      ├─ OptimizerRule
      │   └─ semantic-preserving logical rewrites
      │      projection pushdown, predicate pushdown, limit pushdown,
      │      expression simplification, join rewrites, subquery decorrelation, ...
      ├─ PhysicalPlanner
      │   └─ ExecutionPlan
      └─ PhysicalOptimizerRule
          └─ physical rewrites
             distribution, ordering, join selection, TopK, pushdown, coalescing, ...
```

DataFusion has analyzer rules, logical optimizer rules, and physical optimizer rules. Analyzer rules make a logical plan valid for later planning, logical optimizer rules rewrite `LogicalPlan`s and expressions while preserving results, and physical optimizer rules rewrite `ExecutionPlan`s while preserving results. The official optimizer guide says DataFusion contains extensive `OptimizerRule`s and `PhysicalOptimizerRule`s that may rewrite plans/expressions so they run faster while computing the same result. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 22.1 Value case

| Optimization family         | Value                                                                  |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| analyzer rules              | make plan valid: type coercion, grouping resolution, function rewrites |
| expression simplification   | replace constants/algebraic no-ops before execution                    |
| predicate pushdown          | fewer rows flow through the plan                                       |
| projection pushdown         | fewer columns scanned/copied/materialized                              |
| limit pushdown              | stop earlier; enable top-K / limited operators                         |
| join reordering             | reduce intermediate result size and runtime                            |
| physical distribution rules | add/remove repartitioning to meet join/aggregate requirements          |
| physical ordering rules     | add/remove sorts, exploit source/order properties                      |
| dynamic filters             | feed runtime TopK/join/aggregate state back into scans to skip work    |
| statistics-aware planning   | better join/order/scan/pruning decisions                               |
| custom rules                | domain-specific rewrites and source-aware improvements                 |

Predicate pushdown moves filters earlier so fewer rows are processed; projection pushdown keeps only needed columns earlier, especially valuable for columnar formats like Parquet; limit pushdown pushes row limits earlier and can replace full sort + limit with TopK-like execution. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 22.2 Optimizer phases

| Phase              | Input                   | Output                            | Rule trait              | Can change semantics?                    |
| ------------------ | ----------------------- | --------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Analyzer           | initial `LogicalPlan`   | valid analyzed `LogicalPlan`      | `AnalyzerRule`          | may resolve/transform to valid semantics |
| Logical optimizer  | valid `LogicalPlan`     | faster equivalent `LogicalPlan`   | `OptimizerRule`         | must preserve result semantics           |
| Physical planner   | optimized `LogicalPlan` | `ExecutionPlan`                   | `PhysicalPlanner`       | lowers semantics to algorithms           |
| Physical optimizer | `ExecutionPlan`         | faster equivalent `ExecutionPlan` | `PhysicalOptimizerRule` | must preserve result semantics           |

DataFusion’s architecture docs describe planning as: analyzer rules enforce semantic rules such as type coercion; optimizer rules rewrite logical plans such as projection/filter pushdown; the physical planner creates an execution plan; physical optimizer rules such as sort and join selection improve that execution plan. ([Docs.rs][3])

---

## 22.3 Analyzer rules

### Role

```text id="rrigaf"
AnalyzerRule:
  initial LogicalPlan
    → semantically valid LogicalPlan
```

`AnalyzerRule`s transform `LogicalPlan`s to make them valid before the rest of the optimizer runs. They differ from `OptimizerRule`s because optimizer rules must preserve existing logical semantics, while analyzer rules may resolve expressions into more specific forms or do type coercion to ensure operand types are valid. Built-in analyzer rule implementors include function rewrites, grouping-function resolution, and type coercion. ([Docs.rs][4])

### Trait shape

```rust id="ep8gef"
use std::fmt::Debug;

use datafusion::common::{config::ConfigOptions, Result};
use datafusion::logical_expr::LogicalPlan;
use datafusion::optimizer::analyzer::AnalyzerRule;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyAnalyzerRule;

impl AnalyzerRule for MyAnalyzerRule {
    fn analyze(
        &self,
        plan: LogicalPlan,
        config: &ConfigOptions,
    ) -> Result<LogicalPlan> {
        // rewrite plan into a semantically valid/analyzed form
        Ok(plan)
    }

    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "my_analyzer_rule"
    }
}
```

The released 54.1.0 `AnalyzerRule` trait requires `analyze(plan, config) -> Result<LogicalPlan>` and `name() -> &str`; use `SessionState::add_analyzer_rule` to register additional analyzer rules. ([Docs.rs][4])

### Analyzer use cases

```text id="j2fj2p"
type coercion
function rewrite, e.g. syntax/operator → function call
grouping function resolution
custom semantic validation
domain-specific expression normalization required before optimizer rules
custom placeholder / parameter semantics
```

### Agent rules

```text id="up2fc6"
Use AnalyzerRule only when the input plan is not yet semantically ready.
Use OptimizerRule for performance-only rewrites.
Analyzer rules may change semantic representation but must preserve user-intended query meaning.
Analyzer rules must run before logical optimizer assumptions are relied on.
```

---

## 22.4 Logical optimizer rules

### Role

```text id="qdx7vx"
OptimizerRule:
  LogicalPlan -> LogicalPlan
  same results, better plan
```

`OptimizerRule` transforms one `LogicalPlan` into another that computes the same result, possibly more efficiently. If no transformation applies, the rule must return the input unchanged; the optimizer calls `rewrite` repeatedly until a fixed point, so returning `Transformed::no` when nothing changed is important. ([Docs.rs][5])

### Trait shape

```rust id="42xwcm"
use datafusion::common::{
    tree_node::Transformed,
    Result,
};
use datafusion::logical_expr::LogicalPlan;
use datafusion::optimizer::{OptimizerConfig, OptimizerRule};

#[derive(Default, Debug)]
struct MyOptimizerRule;

impl OptimizerRule for MyOptimizerRule {
    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "my_optimizer_rule"
    }

    fn rewrite(
        &self,
        plan: LogicalPlan,
        config: &dyn OptimizerConfig,
    ) -> Result<Transformed<LogicalPlan>> {
        // Return Transformed::yes(new_plan) if changed.
        // Return Transformed::no(plan) if unchanged.
        Ok(Transformed::no(plan))
    }
}
```

The `OptimizerRule` trait exposes `name`, `apply_order`, `supports_rewrite` (deprecated), and `rewrite`; docs warn rules should avoid function-name-specific transformations because UDFs can override names and semantics, and should use function implementation traits where possible. ([Docs.rs][5])

---

## 22.5 Physical optimizer rules

### Role

```text id="csiaj0"
PhysicalOptimizerRule:
  Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan> -> Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>
  same results, better executable plan
```

`PhysicalOptimizerRule` transforms an `ExecutionPlan` into a more efficient plan that computes the same results. Required methods are `optimize(plan, config)`, `name()`, and `schema_check()`. `schema_check()` tells the physical optimizer whether to validate that the rule did not change the plan schema; some rules may alter nullable properties and should disable schema checking. ([Docs.rs][6])

### Trait shape

```rust id="0ybkwv"
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::common::{config::ConfigOptions, Result};
use datafusion::physical_optimizer::PhysicalOptimizerRule;
use datafusion::physical_plan::ExecutionPlan;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyPhysicalRule;

impl PhysicalOptimizerRule for MyPhysicalRule {
    fn optimize(
        &self,
        plan: Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>,
        config: &ConfigOptions,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        Ok(plan)
    }

    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "my_physical_rule"
    }

    fn schema_check(&self) -> bool {
        true
    }
}
```

The physical optimizer module includes rules for limit pushdown, projection pushdown, sort pushdown, sanity checking, aggregation-related optimizations, and output/distribution requirements; the module docs also state that `SanityCheckPlan` rejects non-runnable plans with infinite sources and checks ordering/distribution requirements. ([Docs.rs][7])

## 22.6 Running the logical optimizer manually

```rust id="yx42jg"
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::logical_expr::{col, lit, LogicalPlan, LogicalPlanBuilder};
use datafusion::optimizer::{Optimizer, OptimizerContext, OptimizerRule};

let initial_logical_plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::empty(false)
    .project(vec![(lit(1i64) + lit(2i64)).alias("x")])?
    .build()?;

let rules: Vec<Arc<dyn OptimizerRule + Send + Sync>> = vec![
    Arc::new(MyOptimizerRule::default()),
];

let optimizer = Optimizer::with_rules(rules);
let config = OptimizerContext::new().with_max_passes(16);

let optimized_plan = optimizer.optimize(
    initial_logical_plan.clone(),
    &config,
    |plan: &LogicalPlan, rule: &dyn OptimizerRule| {
        println!("after {}:\n{}", rule.name(), plan.display_indent());
    },
)?;
```

The optimizer guide demonstrates creating an optimizer with custom rules, using `OptimizerContext::new().with_max_passes(16)`, and supplying an observer callback that prints the plan after each rule application. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

## 22.7 Registering custom rules in `SessionState`

```rust id="8p3y41"
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::execution::session_state::SessionStateBuilder;
use datafusion::prelude::*;

let state = SessionStateBuilder::new()
    .with_default_features()
    .with_optimizer_rule(Arc::new(MyOptimizerRule::default()))
    .with_physical_optimizer_rule(Arc::new(MyPhysicalRule))
    .build();

let ctx = SessionContext::from(state);
```

`OptimizerRule` docs say additional logical optimizer rules can be registered on `SessionState`; physical optimizer docs similarly state additional `PhysicalOptimizerRule`s can be registered on `SessionState`. In codebases using `SessionStateBuilder`, prefer central rule registration during engine construction rather than ad hoc mutation after queries are planned. ([Docs.rs][5])

## 22.8 Rule ordering and fixed points

```text id="mb92dh"
optimizer pass:
  for rule in rules:
    apply rule
    if changed:
      continue
  repeat until fixed point or max passes
```

`OptimizerRule::rewrite` docs state the optimizer calls `rewrite` several times until a fixed point is reached, so rules must return `Transformed::no` when the output is unchanged. `OptimizerRule::apply_order()` can specify how the rule should be applied; if it returns `None`, the rule must handle recursion itself. ([Docs.rs][5])

Agent rules:

```text id="jx92hk"
Return Transformed::no for no-op.
Avoid oscillating rewrites: A -> B -> A.
Keep rules idempotent when possible.
Use max_passes as a guard, not as a correctness crutch.
Rule order matters when rules expose opportunities for later rules.
```

---

## 22.9 Expression rewrites and constant folding

### Example rewrite: `BETWEEN` → comparisons

```rust id="7owrcv"
use datafusion::common::{
    tree_node::{Transformed, TreeNode},
    Result,
};
use datafusion::logical_expr::{Between, Expr};

fn rewrite_between(expr: Expr) -> Result<Transformed<Expr>> {
    expr.transform_up(|expr| {
        let Expr::Between(Between {
            negated,
            expr,
            low,
            high,
        }) = expr
        else {
            return Ok(Transformed::no(expr));
        };

        if negated {
            Ok(Transformed::no(Expr::Between(Between::new(
                expr, negated, low, high,
            ))))
        } else {
            let rewritten = expr.clone()
                .gt_eq(*low)
                .and(expr.lt_eq(*high));

            Ok(Transformed::yes(rewritten))
        }
    })
}
```

The optimizer guide shows this `BETWEEN` rewrite pattern using the `TreeNode` API and `transform_up`, and it also shows `EXPLAIN VERBOSE` demonstrating type coercion and expression simplification reducing `CAST(1 + 2.2 AS string)` into the constant `"3.2"`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Expression-name preservation

```rust id="sua60y"
// Semantically simplify:
lit(1i64) + lit(2i64)  ->  lit(3i64)

// But preserve output field name:
lit(3i64).alias("Int64(1) + Int64(2)")
```

DataFusion identifies columns by expression names inside logical plans, subqueries, and output schemas, so optimizer rewrites must preserve expression names. The optimizer guide explicitly says expression names must not change when rewriting expressions, typically by adding an alias; it shows `1 + 2` optimized to `3 AS "1 + 2"`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text id="q5q8vs"
Use canonical_name for expression equivalence.
Use display_name for schema/output field names.
When simplifying an output expression, alias it to the original display name.
Do not drop aliases in optimizer rewrites.
Do not duplicate volatile expressions.
```

## 22.10 Predicate / filter pushdown

### Logical purpose

```text id="04p2qq"
Filter above expensive plan:
  Aggregate
    Filter(city = 'BOSTON')
      Scan

better:
  Aggregate
    Scan with filter city = 'BOSTON'
```

Predicate pushdown moves filters down so they run earlier; the optimizer blog notes that earlier filtering reduces work for the rest of the plan and can combine with partition/storage pruning. It gives the example of pushing a `HAVING city = 'BOSTON'` predicate before aggregation because filtering first avoids computing all cities. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

### TableProvider interaction

```rust id="tmx28u"
fn supports_filters_pushdown(
    &self,
    filters: &[&Expr],
) -> Result<Vec<TableProviderFilterPushDown>> {
    Ok(filters.iter().map(|f| {
        if source_can_exactly_apply(f) {
            TableProviderFilterPushDown::Exact
        } else if source_can_prune_partitions(f) {
            TableProviderFilterPushDown::Inexact
        } else {
            TableProviderFilterPushDown::Unsupported
        }
    }).collect())
}
```

### Agent rules

```text id="vvdnnn"
Exact pushdown: source enforces predicate exactly; residual filter can be removed.
Inexact pushdown: source prunes candidates; DataFusion must retain residual FilterExec.
Unsupported: DataFusion evaluates the filter.
Do not claim Exact unless SQL null semantics are preserved.
```

---

## 22.11 Projection pushdown

### Logical purpose

```text id="i3dfc8"
Projection high in plan:
  Projection(a)
    Filter(b > 10)
      Scan(a,b,c,d,e)

better:
  Projection(a)
    Filter(b > 10)
      Scan(a,b)   -- c,d,e not needed
```

Projection pushdown moves column narrowing earlier so unused columns are not copied/scanned/materialized. The optimizer blog emphasizes this is especially powerful for columnar storage such as Parquet, where readers can fetch only required columns; it is still useful but less effective for row formats such as JSON/CSV. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

### Physical projection pushdown

The physical optimizer module documents `ProjectionPushdown`, which tries to push projections down through physical operators, and if a projection reaches a source it can disappear from the plan entirely. ([Docs.rs][7])

### Agent rules

```text id="8jaebp"
Avoid SELECT * in generated SQL.
Track columns needed by final projection, filters, joins, group keys, sorts, windows.
Custom TableProvider must map projection indices to remote selected fields.
For nested Parquet, project nested leaves where supported.
```

---

## 22.12 Limit pushdown and TopK

### Logical purpose

```text id="eefk4p"
Full sort + limit:
  Limit 10
    Sort by ts DESC
      Scan all rows

TopK / limit-aware:
  TopK 10 by ts DESC
    Scan with early-stop / dynamic pruning where possible
```

Limit pushdown pushes row limits earlier so the plan can stop generating data sooner. The optimizer blog notes a classic example: replacing a full sort + limit with a TopK operator that tracks only top values using a heap, and that DataFusion’s Parquet reader can stop opening more files once a limit has been hit. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

### Config knobs

```sql id="dk099e"
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_topk_aggregation = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_topk_repartition = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_topk_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_window_topn = false;
```

The configuration docs include top-K-related flags: `enable_topk_aggregation`, `enable_topk_repartition`, `enable_topk_dynamic_filter_pushdown`, and `enable_window_topn`; `enable_window_topn` is false by default and can improve low-cardinality partitioned row-number patterns but may regress high-cardinality cases. ([Apache DataFusion][8])

### Agent rules

```text id="9x4gga"
ORDER BY + LIMIT is a top-K candidate.
Add deterministic tie-breakers for correctness.
Do not assume LIMIT without ORDER BY means top-K.
For window row_number filters, test enable_window_topn under workload cardinality.
```

---

## 22.13 Dynamic filter pushdown

### Concept

```text id="sf892g"
Runtime operator state:
  TopK current cutoff
  Join build-side key/range/filter state
  Aggregate state

→ dynamic filter

→ scan operator / file scan
  skip files / row groups / pages / rows that cannot match current runtime constraint
```

DataFusion’s config docs describe dynamic filters as filters generated by operators such as TopK, Join, and Aggregate and pushed into the file scan phase; the example is `ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 10`, where once the current TopK contains 10 timestamps from 2025, files containing only 2024 timestamps can be skipped. The same config group includes umbrella `enable_dynamic_filter_pushdown` plus specific TopK, join, and aggregate dynamic filter flags. ([Apache DataFusion][8])

### Config

```sql id="6gk28x"
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_topk_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_aggregate_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
```

`enable_dynamic_filter_pushdown` suppresses or overrides the component-specific dynamic-filter flags according to the config docs; treat it as the umbrella control in service profiles. ([Apache DataFusion][8])

### TopK dynamic filter value case

The 2025 dynamic-filter blog reports that TopK dynamic filters improved a common “last K traces” pattern by more than 10x in one motivating production-like workflow, and its example shows TopK passing a current timestamp threshold to scans so files/rows outside the current candidate range can be skipped. ([Apache DataFusion][9])

### Agent rules

```text id="1slm7d"
Dynamic filters help most when:
  scan source has pruning metadata
  query has ORDER BY LIMIT / selective join / aggregate-derived constraints
  source can skip files/row groups/pages

Dynamic filters help less when:
  source cannot prune
  data is unsorted/random relative to dynamic predicate
  predicate column has no useful metadata
  overhead exceeds skipped work
```

## 22.14 Join optimization and cost-based choices

### Config examples

```sql id="953btw"
SET datafusion.optimizer.repartition_joins = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.filter_null_join_keys = false;
```

The configuration docs state that join-related optimizer settings influence algorithm selection; `repartition_joins` enables repartitioning by join keys to execute joins in parallel, and `filter_null_join_keys` can insert filters before joins between nullable and non-nullable join columns but may add overhead when the file format does not fully support predicate pushdown. ([Apache DataFusion][8])

### Join reordering / cost-based planning concept

```text id="iwii54"
Inputs:
  statistics:
    row counts
    byte sizes
    column min/max / distinct estimates
  predicates:
    join keys
    filters
  config:
    join algorithm preferences
    repartition settings
    null-key filtering
Output:
  join order
  join algorithm
  repartition/sort requirements
```

Statistics matter for join ordering and cost-based choices. DataFusion’s architecture docs state physical plans include concrete execution choices such as hash vs merge join and partitioning/sortedness, while `PruningPredicate` and statistical information can prove some filters can never be true. ([Docs.rs][3])

### Agent rules

```text id="na918c"
Expose accurate TableProvider statistics if building custom sources.
Keep join keys typed and cast-compatible.
Prefer equality predicates for hash/repartition joins.
Avoid hiding join keys inside functions when source/optimizer cannot reason about them.
Test join plans under EXPLAIN for large-table workloads.
```

## 22.15 Statistics

### Sources

```text id="bvkgcm"
TableProvider::statistics()
Parquet metadata statistics
catalog/metastore row counts
custom provider estimates
runtime metrics from EXPLAIN ANALYZE
```

Statistics support pruning, cost decisions, and custom optimizer rules. DataFusion’s architecture notes that pruning predicates can prove filters can never be true using statistical information, and the optimizer configs include several statistics-sensitive optimizations such as Parquet pruning and dynamic scan filters. ([Docs.rs][3])

### Agent rules

```text id="dxynfe"
Unknown statistics are safer than wrong exact statistics.
Use conservative estimates for custom providers.
Expose min/max/null counts only if semantics are reliable.
Refresh stale catalog statistics deliberately.
Avoid leaking sensitive distribution metadata through public information_schema or diagnostics.
```

## 22.16 Cost-based vs rule-based optimization

| Type              | Example                                                                     | Input required                            |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| always-good rule  | expression simplification, projection pushdown, predicate pushdown          | plan shape/expression semantics           |
| cost-aware choice | join reordering, join algorithm choice, repartitioning, file repartitioning | statistics, config, physical properties   |
| runtime/dynamic   | dynamic filter pushdown                                                     | operator runtime state + scan integration |

The optimizer blog classifies expression simplification, predicate pushdown, and limit pushdown as “always optimizations” that are generally always worth doing, while other choices depend more heavily on workload, statistics, and physical layout. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

Agent rules:

```text id="2vsi8a"
Always-on rules should be semantic-preserving and broadly beneficial.
Cost-aware rules must degrade safely when stats are unknown.
Runtime/dynamic rules need source/operator integration and metrics.
```

## 22.18 Custom logical optimizer rule: expression simplifier example

```rust id="7y7rii"
use datafusion::common::{
    tree_node::{Transformed, TreeNode},
    Result,
};
use datafusion::logical_expr::{Expr, LogicalPlan};
use datafusion::optimizer::{OptimizerConfig, OptimizerRule};

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct RewriteBetweenRule;

impl OptimizerRule for RewriteBetweenRule {
    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "rewrite_between_rule"
    }

    fn rewrite(
        &self,
        plan: LogicalPlan,
        _config: &dyn OptimizerConfig,
    ) -> Result<Transformed<LogicalPlan>> {
        plan.transform_up(|plan| {
            let transformed = plan.map_expressions(|expr| rewrite_between(expr))?;
            Ok(transformed)
        })
    }
}

fn rewrite_between(expr: Expr) -> Result<Transformed<Expr>> {
    expr.transform_up(|expr| {
        if let Expr::Between(between) = expr {
            if between.negated {
                return Ok(Transformed::no(Expr::Between(between)));
            }

            let rewritten = between.expr.clone()
                .gt_eq(*between.low)
                .and(between.expr.lt_eq(*between.high));

            // If this expression contributes to an output schema, preserve name at caller layer.
            Ok(Transformed::yes(rewritten))
        } else {
            Ok(Transformed::no(expr))
        }
    })
}
```

The `TreeNode` API is the documented approach for walking and rewriting expression and plan trees; the optimizer guide’s `BETWEEN` example uses bottom-up `transform_up` to rewrite expressions while returning `Transformed::yes` or `Transformed::no`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

```rust id="qn87v8"
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::common::{config::ConfigOptions, Result};
use datafusion::physical_optimizer::PhysicalOptimizerRule;
use datafusion::physical_plan::ExecutionPlan;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct RemoveMyNoOpExec;

impl PhysicalOptimizerRule for RemoveMyNoOpExec {
    fn optimize(
        &self,
        plan: Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>,
        config: &ConfigOptions,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        // transform ExecutionPlan tree;
        // preserve schema and physical semantics
        Ok(plan)
    }

    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "remove_my_noop_exec"
    }

    fn schema_check(&self) -> bool {
        true
    }
}
```

`PhysicalOptimizerRule::schema_check()` should generally be true; disable it only when a rule intentionally changes nullable schema properties and has tests proving downstream correctness. ([Docs.rs][6])

## 22.20 TableProvider pushdown integration

### Pushdown contract

```rust id="gjpnuw"
fn supports_filters_pushdown(
    &self,
    filters: &[&Expr],
) -> Result<Vec<TableProviderFilterPushDown>> {
    Ok(filters.iter().map(|f| {
        if self.can_apply_exactly(f) {
            TableProviderFilterPushDown::Exact
        } else if self.can_prune_candidates(f) {
            TableProviderFilterPushDown::Inexact
        } else {
            TableProviderFilterPushDown::Unsupported
        }
    }).collect())
}

async fn scan(
    &self,
    state: &dyn Session,
    projection: Option<&Vec<usize>>,
    filters: &[Expr],
    limit: Option<usize>,
) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
    // build custom ExecutionPlan with pushed projection/filter/limit
}
```

The optimizer can only push predicates/projections/limits into custom sources if the provider exposes accurate capabilities and `scan` implements the corresponding behavior; false `Exact` declarations can produce wrong answers, while conservative `Unsupported` leaves optimization on the table.

### Agent rules

```text id="7k12uv"
Projection pushdown: return only requested columns in requested order.
Exact predicate pushdown: source enforces predicate exactly.
Inexact predicate pushdown: source prunes but residual DataFusion filter remains.
Limit pushdown: unsafe with inexact filters unless over-fetching preserves semantics.
Statistics: expose conservative row/byte/cardinality estimates when available.
```

## 22.21 Debugging optimizer behavior

### `EXPLAIN`

```sql id="8qp6rb"
EXPLAIN
SELECT city, COUNT(*)
FROM population
GROUP BY city
HAVING city = 'BOSTON';
```

### `EXPLAIN VERBOSE`

```sql id="asxku7"
EXPLAIN VERBOSE
SELECT CAST(1 + 2.2 AS STRING) AS foo;
```

`EXPLAIN VERBOSE` shows the effect of each optimization rule. The optimizer guide shows `type_coercion` inserting a cast and `simplify_expressions` reducing a casted arithmetic expression to a constant. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`

```sql id="mu318z"
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT *
FROM hits
WHERE "URL" LIKE '%google%'
ORDER BY "EventTime"
LIMIT 10;
```

Use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` for runtime metrics after physical optimization; use `EXPLAIN VERBOSE` for logical/physical rewrite visibility. The optimizer guide specifically recommends `EXPLAIN VERBOSE` for seeing the effect of each optimizer rule. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 22.22 Rule testing strategy

The optimizer guide recommends unit tests in the same file as a new rule to test the rule in isolation and an integration test to test the rule as part of the overall optimization process. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Unit test: isolated rule

```rust id="3xpd1z"
#[test]
fn my_rule_rewrites_expected_plan() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let plan = make_input_plan()?;
    let rule = MyOptimizerRule::default();

    let transformed = rule.rewrite(plan, &OptimizerContext::new())?;
    assert!(transformed.transformed);

    let plan = transformed.data;
    assert_eq!(plan.display_indent().to_string(), expected);

    plan.check_invariants()?;
    Ok(())
}
```

### Integration test: optimizer pipeline

```rust id="5rtx3m"
#[tokio::test]
async fn my_rule_in_optimizer_pipeline() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = make_context_with_rule();

    let df = ctx.sql("SELECT ...").await?;
    let optimized = df.clone().into_optimized_plan()?;

    insta::assert_snapshot!(optimized.display_indent().to_string());

    let batches = df.collect().await?;
    assert_batches_eq!(expected, &batches);

    Ok(())
}
```

### Required test matrix

```text id="gemw2a"
[ ] no-op input returns Transformed::no
[ ] matching input returns Transformed::yes
[ ] rule is idempotent or converges
[ ] plan.check_invariants()
[ ] schema preserved
[ ] output expression names preserved
[ ] aliases preserved
[ ] volatile functions not duplicated/reordered
[ ] optimizer with full rule set still produces correct results
[ ] EXPLAIN VERBOSE includes expected transformation
```

---

## 22.23 Rule-ordering hazards

```text id="b4r5vy"
Rule A creates pattern for Rule B:
  A: simplify expression
  B: predicate pushdown

Rule B removes pattern expected by Rule C:
  B: projection pushdown
  C: domain-specific rewrite

Rule D oscillates:
  D1: rewrite X -> Y
  D2: rewrite Y -> X
```

Agent rules:

```text id="wmjrio"
Place domain-specific rules after analyzer/type coercion.
Place rules before physical planning if they change logical shape.
Avoid relying on display strings as matching keys.
Match on Expr/LogicalPlan structure.
Use observer callbacks and EXPLAIN VERBOSE to debug rule order.
```

---

## 22.24 Optimizer rule deployment profiles

### Default engine

```rust id="0yc0mu"
let ctx = SessionContext::new();
```

Use built-in rules unless a product-specific rule has a measured benefit.

### Domain-specific optimizer

```rust id="q6td27"
let state = SessionStateBuilder::new()
    .with_default_features()
    .with_optimizer_rule(Arc::new(MyDomainRule))
    .build();

let ctx = SessionContext::from(state);
```

### Locked-down deterministic testing

```rust id="ca0l5g"
let optimizer = Optimizer::with_rules(vec![
    Arc::new(MyRuleA),
    Arc::new(MyRuleB),
]);

let config = OptimizerContext::new().with_max_passes(4);
```

Agent rules:

```text id="9jvnz6"
Use built-ins by default.
Add rules only with benchmark or correctness motivation.
Keep rule sets small and explainable in product engines.
Pin DataFusion version for rule APIs and plan snapshots.
```

## 22.25 Optimizer and custom extensions

### Custom `TableProvider`

```text id="bfrpr6"
Expose:
  projection pushdown
  predicate pushdown
  limit support
  statistics
  partitioning/order properties
```

### Custom logical node

```text id="1q2ap8"
Expose:
  schema()
  inputs()
  expressions()
  with_exprs_and_inputs()
  projection/predicate/limit pushdown hooks if safe
```

### Custom physical node

```text id="l7fc8x"
Expose:
  PlanProperties
  children()
  with_new_children()
  metrics()
  schema-preserving rewrites
```

DataFusion’s architecture docs list custom plan rewrite passes alongside custom `TableProvider`s, logical plans, functions, physical operators, and custom planners; the optimizer depends on extension nodes correctly exposing schema, expressions, inputs, and physical properties. ([Docs.rs][3])

---

## 22.26 Deployment advisory

```text id="k2c3j8"
Production:
  keep default optimizer enabled
  explicitly configure only measured toggles
  capture EXPLAIN plans for critical queries
  capture EXPLAIN ANALYZE metrics for regressions
  expose table statistics conservatively
  test custom providers with pushdown on/off
  pin DataFusion version for custom rules

Multi-tenant service:
  optimizer can rewrite user queries across views/providers
  enforce authorization before/after optimization where needed
  ensure pushed filters do not bypass row/column policies
  do not leak stats through public metadata if sensitive

Custom source:
  implement pushdown conservatively
  use Inexact when residual filter is required
  validate pushed limit interactions
  provide stats only when reliable
```

---

## 22.27 Anti-pattern inventory

* Returning `Transformed::yes` when the plan is unchanged.
* Changing expression names during rewrites.
* Dropping aliases during expression simplification.
* Matching function names instead of function implementation semantics.
* Rewriting volatile expressions as if deterministic.
* Claiming exact predicate pushdown for approximate remote filters.
* Pushing `LIMIT` below inexact filters unsafely.
* Relying on stale/wrong statistics as exact.
* Adding custom rules without result-equivalence tests.
* Snapshotting physical plan strings across versions without pinning.
* Disabling optimizer rules globally to work around one query bug.
* Assuming dynamic filters help when the source cannot prune.
* Enabling `enable_window_topn` blindly for high-cardinality partitions.
* Writing physical optimizer rules that change schema while `schema_check()` returns true.
* Implementing custom logical nodes without correct `with_exprs_and_inputs`.

---

```text id="v3vb7p"
[ ] Identify phase: AnalyzerRule / OptimizerRule / PhysicalOptimizerRule.
[ ] Analyzer rules make plans valid; optimizer rules preserve results.
[ ] Use TreeNode apply/transform APIs for plan/expression traversal.
[ ] Preserve expression names with aliases after rewrites.
[ ] Return Transformed::no for no-op rewrites.
[ ] Avoid function-name-specific rewrites; respect UDF override semantics.
[ ] Use EXPLAIN VERBOSE to inspect rule effects.
[ ] Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to inspect runtime effects.
[ ] Tune optimizer configs only with workload evidence.
[ ] Implement TableProvider pushdown accurately: Exact/Inexact/Unsupported.
[ ] Expose conservative statistics for cost-aware choices.
[ ] Test join/order/limit/pushdown interactions.
[ ] Test custom rules in isolation and in full optimizer pipeline.
[ ] Pin DataFusion version for custom optimizer APIs and plan snapshots.
[ ] Treat dynamic filters and TopK as source-layout-dependent optimizations.
```

## 22.29 Statistics-driven Top-K and new optimizer switches (DataFusion 54)

### Statistics-driven Top-K ordering and early termination

DataFusion 54 makes `ORDER BY ... LIMIT k` (Top-K) plans exploit **file/column statistics**: when statistics prove which files or partitions can possibly contribute to the top k rows, scan order is arranged to read the most promising data first, and execution terminates early once the Top-K heap provably cannot change (the running threshold also feeds the pre-existing dynamic-filter machinery, which improved in 54 rather than being introduced by it — the `*_dynamic_filter_pushdown` keys already existed in 53). Sorted-by-time telemetry with `ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT n` is the flagship case: recent files are read first and older files are skipped entirely.

### New optimizer configuration keys in 54

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_topk_repartition = true;   -- default true
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_window_topn = false;        -- default false
SET datafusion.optimizer.join_reordering = true;            -- default true
SET datafusion.optimizer.use_statistics_registry = false;   -- default false
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_unions_to_filter = false;   -- default false
```

| Key | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `enable_topk_repartition` | `true` | allows repartitioning below a Top-K so partial Top-K runs in parallel before the final merge |
| `enable_window_topn` | `false` | opt-in rewrite of `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) <= n`-style window filters into Top-N execution |
| `join_reordering` | `true` | statistics-informed join-order selection in the optimizer |
| `use_statistics_registry` | `false` | opt-in registry-backed statistics source for planning (experimental) |
| `enable_unions_to_filter` | `false` | opt-in `UnionsToFilter` rule: rewrites `UNION ALL` branches over the same source that differ only by predicate into a single scan with an OR-filter |

The `UnionsToFilter` rule (`datafusion_optimizer::unions_to_filter::UnionsToFilter`) ships in 54 but is **disabled by default** — enable it deliberately and verify plans, since collapsing unions changes partitioning and ordering properties of the plan.

Agent rules:

```text
Keep statistics collection on for Top-K-heavy workloads; early termination depends on it.
enable_window_topn and enable_unions_to_filter are opt-in: test plans before enabling in production.
Do not present the *_dynamic_filter_pushdown keys as new in 54; they pre-date it (behavior improved).
Re-baseline EXPLAIN snapshots: Top-K/repartition shapes changed between 53 and 54.
```

# DataFusion Advanced — 23) Join algorithms and join tuning

Style target follows the uploaded advanced-reference pattern. 

## 23.0 Join mental model

```text
SQL / DataFrame join
  → LogicalPlan::Join
      ├─ JoinType
      ├─ equijoin keys
      ├─ optional non-equi join filter
      └─ output projection/schema
  → logical optimizer
      ├─ predicate pushdown
      ├─ projection pushdown
      ├─ join reordering / null-key filtering
      └─ join predicate extraction
  → physical planner / physical optimizer
      ├─ HashJoinExec
      ├─ SortMergeJoinExec
      ├─ NestedLoopJoinExec
      ├─ PiecewiseMergeJoinExec
      ├─ SymmetricHashJoinExec
      └─ CrossJoinExec
  → ExecutionPlan::execute(partition, TaskContext)
      → SendableRecordBatchStream
```

DataFusion’s SQL reference documents inner, left/right/full outer, natural, cross, left/right semi, left/right anti, lateral, and left lateral joins. Its physical join module includes `HashJoinExec`, `SortMergeJoinExec`, `NestedLoopJoinExec`, `PiecewiseMergeJoinExec`, `SymmetricHashJoinExec`, and `CrossJoinExec`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 23.1 SQL join syntax map

### Inner join

```sql
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  c.customer_name
FROM orders AS o
INNER JOIN customers AS c
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
```

Inner joins return rows with matches on both sides. Use for normal equijoin relationships. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Left outer join

```sql
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  o.order_id
FROM customers AS c
LEFT OUTER JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Left outer joins preserve all left rows and fill right columns with `NULL` where no match exists. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Right outer join

```sql
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  o.order_id
FROM customers AS c
RIGHT OUTER JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Right outer joins preserve all right rows and fill left columns with `NULL` where no match exists. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Full outer join

```sql
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  o.order_id
FROM customers AS c
FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Full outer joins preserve unmatched rows from both inputs, filling the missing side with `NULL`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Cross join

```sql
SELECT
  a.id AS a_id,
  b.id AS b_id
FROM a
CROSS JOIN b;
```

A cross join returns the Cartesian product. DataFusion’s `CrossJoinExec` buffers the left input in memory and streams right-side batches while combining them with the buffered left side. ([Docs.rs][2])

### Natural join

```sql
SELECT *
FROM x NATURAL JOIN y;
```

A natural join is an inner join based on common column names; if no common column names exist, DataFusion documents that it behaves like a cross join. Avoid natural joins in generated SQL unless the schema is tightly controlled. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Semi join

```sql
SELECT *
FROM customers AS c
LEFT SEMI JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Semi joins return rows from one side that have a match on the other side and project only the preserved side’s columns. Use for existence predicates. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Anti join

```sql
SELECT *
FROM customers AS c
LEFT ANTI JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Anti joins return rows from one side with no match on the other side and project only the preserved side’s columns. Use for non-existence predicates. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Lateral join

```sql
SELECT
  d.name AS department,
  e.name AS employee
FROM departments AS d,
LATERAL (
  SELECT employees.name
  FROM employees
  WHERE employees.dept_id = d.id
) AS e;
```

DataFusion requires the `LATERAL` keyword for correlated subqueries in `FROM`; the docs also document `LEFT JOIN LATERAL` and note limitations for outer references in lateral subquery `SELECT` lists and `HAVING`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 23.2 DataFrame join syntax

### Equijoin by column names

```rust
use datafusion::logical_expr::JoinType;
use datafusion::prelude::*;

let joined = left.join(
    right,
    JoinType::Inner,
    &["customer_id"],
    &["customer_id"],
    None,
)?;
```

### Expression join

```rust
let joined = left.join_on(
    right,
    JoinType::Inner,
    [
        col("orders.customer_id").eq(col("customers.id")),
        col("orders.region").eq(col("customers.region")),
    ],
)?;
```

### Outer join

```rust
let joined = left.join(
    right,
    JoinType::Left,
    &["customer_id"],
    &["customer_id"],
    None,
)?;
```

### Semi / anti join

```rust
let semi = left.join(
    right.clone(),
    JoinType::LeftSemi,
    &["customer_id"],
    &["customer_id"],
    None,
)?;

let anti = left.join(
    right,
    JoinType::LeftAnti,
    &["customer_id"],
    &["customer_id"],
    None,
)?;
```

Agent rules:

```text
Use join(...) for simple equijoins.
Use join_on(...) for generated composite predicates.
Use semi/anti joins for EXISTS / NOT EXISTS style logic.
Always disambiguate duplicate column names before or immediately after joins.
Use qualified columns after joining tables that share field names.
```

---

## 23.3 Logical join anatomy

```text
LogicalPlan::Join
  left: LogicalPlan
  right: LogicalPlan
  join_type: JoinType
  join_constraint: On | Using
  on: Vec<(left_col, right_col)>
  filter: Option<Expr>
  projection: Option<Vec<usize>>
  null_equality: NullEqualsNull | NullEqualsNothing
```

Physical join operators typically split predicates into **equijoin keys** and **join filters**. For example, `HashJoinExec` stores equijoin columns in `on` and non-equality filters in `filter`; `SortMergeJoinExec` similarly represents equijoin predicates separately from optional post-equi join filters. ([Docs.rs][3])

Example:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a
JOIN b
  ON a.id = b.id
 AND a.ts < b.expires_at;
```

Conceptual split:

```text
equijoin key:
  a.id = b.id

join filter:
  a.ts < b.expires_at
```

Agent rules:

```text
Equijoin keys enable hash join / sort-merge join.
Non-equi predicates become join filters or specialized range joins.
Avoid wrapping join keys in functions when a direct equality predicate is possible.
Prefer explicit ON predicates over NATURAL JOIN in generated SQL.
```

---

## 23.4 Physical join algorithm map

| Physical operator        | Best for                                                    | Main risk                                 |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `HashJoinExec`           | equijoins, enough memory for build side                     | build-side memory pressure                |
| `SortMergeJoinExec`      | equijoins with sorted inputs or memory-limited large inputs | sort cost / ordering requirements         |
| `NestedLoopJoinExec`     | non-equi joins without equijoin keys                        | O(left × right) cost; buffers left        |
| `PiecewiseMergeJoinExec` | single range predicate joins                                | experimental; sorted/buffered constraints |
| `SymmetricHashJoinExec`  | streaming/unbounded joins with range/window pruning         | buffer pruning correctness                |
| `CrossJoinExec`          | intentional Cartesian product                               | explosive output; buffers left            |

DataFusion’s join module documents these physical join implementations and their intended roles; notably, `HashJoinExec` evaluates equijoin predicates with hash tables, `SortMergeJoinExec` can join arbitrarily large sorted inputs, `NestedLoopJoinExec` targets joins without equijoin keys, `PiecewiseMergeJoinExec` targets a single range filter, and `SymmetricHashJoinExec` targets streaming contexts with hash tables on both sides. ([Docs.rs][4])

---

## 23.5 Hash join

### Physical role

```text
HashJoinExec
  left child  = build side
  right child = probe side
  on          = equijoin key pairs
  filter      = optional join filter
  join_type   = INNER / LEFT / RIGHT / FULL / SEMI / ANTI / ...
  mode        = PartitionMode
```

DataFusion documents the `HashJoinExec` left child as the build side and the right child as the probe side. The build side is hashed into a table; the probe side is filtered by that hash table. DataFusion explicitly warns that putting the smaller input on the build side is very important to minimize hash-table creation work. ([Docs.rs][3])

### SQL shape

```sql
SELECT *
FROM small_dim AS d
JOIN large_fact AS f
  ON d.id = f.dim_id;
```

Preferred physical build/probe intent:

```text
build side: small_dim
probe side: large_fact
```

### Config

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = true;
```

`datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join` defaults to `true`; when true, the optimizer favors hash join for faster execution when sufficient memory is available, and when false, it may choose sort-merge join when more memory-efficient execution is needed. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

### Rust config

```rust
let mut config = SessionConfig::new();
config.set_bool("datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join", true)?;
let ctx = SessionContext::new_with_config(config);
```

### Agent tuning rules

```text
Good hash join:
  equality keys
  smaller build side
  enough memory for build hash table
  useful projection pushdown before join
  low-to-moderate duplicate explosion

Risky hash join:
  large build side
  skewed join keys
  high duplicate multiplicity
  wide build rows
  insufficient memory
```

### Build/probe side correction

```sql
-- Usually better if dim is smaller:
SELECT *
FROM dim
JOIN fact
  ON dim.id = fact.dim_id;
```

If the optimizer chooses the wrong build side, inspect statistics and physical plan. `HashJoinExec` exposes `swap_inputs`, and the docs note DataFusion’s default SQL interface uses this through the `JoinSelection` physical optimizer before distribution enforcement inserts repartitioning operators. ([Docs.rs][3])

---

## 23.6 Hash join partitioning and repartitioning

### Config

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.repartition_joins = true;
```

`repartition_joins` enables repartitioning joined data by join keys so joins can execute in parallel. Hash join has a `PartitionMode`; DataFusion’s docs note that partitioned hash join can split the build side across partitions, affecting optimizations such as dense-key array-map optimization. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

### Conceptual plan

```text
HashJoinExec
  RepartitionExec hash(left_key)
    left input
  RepartitionExec hash(right_key)
    right input
```

### Agent rules

```text
Enable repartition_joins for large parallel equijoins.
Avoid unnecessary repartitioning for tiny joins.
Expose accurate source partitioning when implementing custom providers.
If inputs are already partitioned on join keys, preserve partition metadata.
Check EXPLAIN for RepartitionExec placement.
```

---

## 23.7 Sort-merge join

### Physical role

```text
SortMergeJoinExec
  left/right inputs must be sorted on join keys
  on = equijoin key pairs
  filter = optional non-equi join filter
  join_type = join semantics
```

`SortMergeJoinExec` executes equijoin predicates on multiple partitions using the sort-merge join algorithm and can be used for arbitrarily large inputs where one or both inputs do not fit in available memory. It assumes both inputs are pre-sorted; sorting inputs is not the responsibility of the execution plan itself. ([Docs.rs][7])

### Config

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = false;
```

When `prefer_hash_join` is false, DataFusion allows sort-merge join to be chosen when more memory-efficient execution is needed. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

### SQL pattern

```sql
SELECT *
FROM left_events AS l
JOIN right_events AS r
  ON l.user_id = r.user_id
ORDER BY l.user_id;
```

### Agent rules

```text
Good sort-merge join:
  inputs already sorted or cheaply sortable
  large inputs exceed hash-table memory
  downstream also needs join-key ordering
  memory-limited workloads

Risk:
  sorting cost can dominate
  wrong ordering metadata can produce incorrect plans
  spilled buffered side can increase disk I/O
```

### Memory behavior

Sort-merge join has streamed and buffered inputs. The streamed side memory depends on output batch size; buffered input is buffered for record batches with the same join key, and if memory limit is exceeded and spilling is enabled, buffered batches can spill to disk; otherwise execution fails. ([Docs.rs][7])

---

## 23.8 Nested loop join

### Physical role

```text
NestedLoopJoinExec
  designed for joins without equijoin keys
  buffers left side
  streams right side
  evaluates join filter over Cartesian candidates
```

`NestedLoopJoinExec` is a build-probe join for joins that do not have equijoin keys in their `ON` clause. It eagerly buffers left-side input batches, and right-side batches are streamed and compared against the buffered left side using the join filter. As of DataFusion 54, `NestedLoopJoinExec` supports memory-limited execution with spilling: when the buffered build side exceeds the memory budget, build-side data spills to disk through the `DiskManager` instead of aborting with an out-of-memory error (in 53 and earlier, a build side that did not fit was a hard OOM). Spilling requires a runtime with memory limits and a configured `DiskManager`; the changelog reports coverage for inner/left and right/full join types. Spill files honor `datafusion.execution.spill_compression` (`uncompressed`, `lz4_frame`, `zstd` — a key that pre-dates 54). ([Docs.rs][8])

### SQL pattern

```sql
SELECT *
FROM ranges AS r
JOIN events AS e
  ON e.ts >= r.start_ts
 AND e.ts < r.end_ts;
```

### Agent rules

```text
Nested loop is fallback for non-equi joins.
Keep left/build side small.
Avoid nested loop on two large tables.
Rewrite to equijoin + residual filter if possible.
Enable piecewise merge join for single range predicates if appropriate.
```

### Memory behavior

Nested loop always considers the left side as the build/buffered side; DataFusion docs say the physical optimizer should assign the smaller input to the left. Output buffering threshold is tied to batch size. Since DataFusion 54, memory-limited execution is implemented: the buffered build side spills to disk under memory pressure (requires memory limits plus a `DiskManager` on the runtime). ([Docs.rs][8])

---

## 23.9 Piecewise merge join

### Physical role

```text
PiecewiseMergeJoinExec
  specialized range join
  single comparison filter:
    <, <=, >, >=
  buffered side sorted
  streamed side sorted during processing
```

`PiecewiseMergeJoinExec` evaluates a single range filter and is documented as much faster than nested-loop join for these workloads. The physical planner may select it when there is exactly one comparison filter with `<`, `<=`, `>`, or `>=`; the buffered side must be sorted according to the operator, while streamed batches can be sorted during processing. ([Docs.rs][9])

### Enable

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_piecewise_merge_join = true;
```

`enable_piecewise_merge_join` defaults to `false` and enables the experimental piecewise merge join algorithm; the config docs state it can be selected when there is exactly one range filter and is faster than nested loop except for some cases where both tables are large and approximately equal in size. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

### SQL patterns

```sql
SELECT *
FROM left_table AS l
JOIN right_table AS r
  ON l.ts < r.ts;
```

```sql
SELECT *
FROM intervals AS i
JOIN events AS e
  ON e.ts >= i.start_ts;
```

### Agent rules

```text
Use only for single range-filter join shapes.
Do not expect it for compound range conditions.
Benchmark before enabling globally.
Prefer equijoin + residual filter when equality keys exist.
Avoid for two similarly large tables without benchmarks.
```

---

## 23.10 Symmetric hash join

### Physical role

```text
SymmetricHashJoinExec
  hash both input streams
  probe both directions
  range conditions can prune stale state
  designed for streaming/unbounded contexts
```

`SymmetricHashJoinExec` hashes both input streams on join keys. DataFusion’s docs describe it as efficient for streaming because it avoids scanning one or both streams for matches and can consider only elements within a sliding window when range conditions are present, enabling operation on unbounded streaming data without unbounded stale state. ([Docs.rs][10])

### Config

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning = true;
```

`allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning` controls whether symmetric hash joins are allowed for unbounded data sources when inputs lack ordering or filtering; disabling it prevents symmetric hash join plans that cannot prune internal buffers and may only produce results at the end. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

### Streaming SQL shape

```sql
SELECT *
FROM left_stream AS l
JOIN right_stream AS r
  ON l.user_id = r.user_id
 AND l.event_ts BETWEEN r.event_ts - INTERVAL '5 minutes'
                    AND r.event_ts + INTERVAL '5 minutes';
```

### Agent rules

```text
Use symmetric hash join for stream-stream joins only when pruning/window constraints exist.
Require time/range predicates or ordering that bounds state.
Avoid unbounded joins with no pruning condition.
Monitor internal buffer growth.
Inspect EXPLAIN for SymmetricHashJoinExec.
```

---

## 23.11 Cross join

### SQL

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a
CROSS JOIN b;
```

`CrossJoinExec` returns the Cartesian product, buffers the left input in memory, then streams right-side batches and combines them with the buffered left input. ([Docs.rs][2])

### Agent rules

```text
Cross join is output-multiplicative: rows = left_rows × right_rows.
Use only when intentional.
Apply filters and projections before cross join.
Use LIMIT only for exploration, not correctness.
Avoid cross joins in generated SQL unless explicitly requested.
```

---

## 23.12 Join filters

### Meaning

```text
Equijoin condition:
  a.id = b.id
  → physical on keys

Join filter:
  a.ts < b.ts
  a.score + b.score > 100
  → optional JoinFilter evaluated after/on match candidates
```

`HashJoinExec` and `SortMergeJoinExec` both expose optional filters; `SortMergeJoinExec` docs describe non-equality predicates as filter expressions evaluated after equijoin predicates. ([Docs.rs][3])

### SQL

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a
JOIN b
  ON a.id = b.id
 AND a.ts < b.ts
 AND a.region = 'us';
```

Optimizer split:

```text
equi keys:
  a.id = b.id

join filter / other pushdown candidates:
  a.ts < b.ts
  a.region = 'us'
```

Agent rules:

```text
Keep equality join keys syntactically visible.
Move single-table predicates to WHERE when possible for pushdown.
Do not hide equijoin keys in CASE/lower/cast unless required.
Non-equi filters can force nested-loop or piecewise/range algorithms.
```

---

## 23.13 Dynamic join filters

### Concept

```text
Runtime join state
  → build-side keys / ranges / min-max
  → dynamic filter
  → scan/probe side pruning
```

DataFusion’s dynamic filter config describes dynamic filters generated by operators such as TopK, Join, and Aggregate and pushed into file scans; `enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown` controls join-derived dynamic filters. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

### Config

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
```

### Good use case

```sql
SELECT *
FROM fact AS f
JOIN small_dim AS d
  ON f.dim_id = d.id
WHERE d.category = 'active';
```

Conceptual runtime effect:

```text
small_dim filtered keys
  → dynamic key/range filter
  → fact scan prunes irrelevant files/row groups/pages if source can use metadata
```

Agent rules:

```text
Dynamic join filters help only if scan source can prune.
Best with Parquet statistics, partition columns, or indexed custom sources.
Less useful for CSV/JSON without metadata.
Enable and benchmark under real file layout.
```

---

## 23.14 Build/probe side concerns

### Hash join

```text
HashJoinExec:
  left  = build side
  right = probe side
```

DataFusion’s `HashJoinExec` docs state the build side is the first child and the probe side is the second child, and smaller input should be placed on the build side to reduce hash-table work. ([Docs.rs][3])

### Nested loop / cross join

```text
NestedLoopJoinExec:
  left = buffered/build side
  right = streamed/probe side

CrossJoinExec:
  left = loaded in memory
  right = streamed/combined with left
```

Nested loop and cross join docs both describe buffering the left input and streaming the right input. ([Docs.rs][8])

### Sort-merge join

```text
SortMergeJoinExec:
  both inputs sorted on join keys
  streamed/probe side determined by join type
  buffered side may spill if spilling enabled
```

Sort-merge join docs describe streamed and buffered sides and note that buffered batches can spill to disk if spilling is enabled and memory is exceeded. ([Docs.rs][7])

### Agent rules

```text
Put smaller side left/build for hash, nested-loop, and cross joins when possible.
Use statistics so optimizer can choose/swap sides.
After repartitioning, avoid manual child swapping unless partition requirements are recomputed.
Project only needed columns before join to reduce build memory.
```

---

## 23.15 Join memory behavior and spilling

| Operator                 | Memory behavior                                                                                 |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `HashJoinExec`           | builds hash table from build side; memory proportional to build rows/width and key multiplicity |
| `SortMergeJoinExec`      | requires sorted inputs; buffers matching-key groups; buffered input can spill if enabled        |
| `NestedLoopJoinExec`     | buffers left side; since DataFusion 54 spills to disk under memory pressure instead of erroring |
| `CrossJoinExec`          | buffers entire left side                                                                        |
| `SymmetricHashJoinExec`  | maintains hash tables for both streams; needs pruning/window constraints to bound memory        |
| `PiecewiseMergeJoinExec` | buffers one sorted side; streams the other                                                      |

Sort-merge join has documented spill behavior for buffered batches; nested-loop join docs currently describe out-of-memory failure when left-side batches cannot fit, with memory-limited fallback as future work. ([Docs.rs][7])

### Runtime config

```rust
use datafusion::execution::{
    runtime_env::RuntimeEnvBuilder,
    session_state::SessionStateBuilder,
};
use datafusion::prelude::*;

let runtime = RuntimeEnvBuilder::new()
    .with_memory_limit(16 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024, 0.8)
    .with_temp_file_path("/mnt/ssd/datafusion-spill")
    .build_arc()?;

let state = SessionStateBuilder::new()
    .with_runtime_env(runtime)
    .with_default_features()
    .build();

let ctx = SessionContext::from(state);
```

### Agent memory rules

```text
Minimize build-side width with projection pushdown.
Filter before join.
Use semi/anti joins for existence checks.
Use sort-merge when memory-limited and sorted/sortable inputs are acceptable.
Avoid nested-loop/cross joins on large inputs.
Configure memory limit and spill path for service/batch workloads.
```

---

## 23.16 Join algorithm configuration

### SQL

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.repartition_joins = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_piecewise_merge_join = false;
SET datafusion.optimizer.allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.filter_null_join_keys = false;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
```

### Rust

```rust
let mut config = SessionConfig::new();

config.set_bool("datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join", true)?;
config.set_bool("datafusion.optimizer.repartition_joins", true)?;
config.set_bool("datafusion.optimizer.enable_piecewise_merge_join", false)?;
config.set_bool(
    "datafusion.optimizer.allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning",
    true,
)?;
config.set_bool("datafusion.optimizer.filter_null_join_keys", false)?;
config.set_bool(
    "datafusion.optimizer.enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown",
    true,
)?;

let ctx = SessionContext::new_with_config(config);
```

The current configuration reference documents join-specific optimizer settings including `allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning`, `prefer_hash_join`, and `enable_piecewise_merge_join`; broader optimizer settings also include join repartitioning, null-key filtering, and dynamic filter pushdown. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

---

## 23.17 Null join-key behavior

### SQL null semantics

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a
JOIN b
  ON a.key = b.key;
```

Default SQL equality does not match `NULL = NULL`. DataFusion physical joins expose `null_equality` / `NullEquality` fields, and `HashJoinExec` docs include null-aware and null-equality fields in its physical operator. ([Docs.rs][3])

### Config

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.filter_null_join_keys = true;
```

`filter_null_join_keys` can insert filters before joins where nullable and non-nullable columns are joined, but the config docs warn it may add overhead when the file format does not fully support predicate pushdown. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

### Agent rules

```text
Do not assume NULL keys match.
Use explicit null-safe logic only if the query semantics require it.
Consider filter_null_join_keys for large joins with many nullable keys.
Benchmark null-key filtering; it can add filters that do not push down well.
```

---

## 23.18 Semi/anti joins as performance tools

### Existence query

```sql
SELECT *
FROM customers AS c
LEFT SEMI JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

### Non-existence query

```sql
SELECT *
FROM customers AS c
LEFT ANTI JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Semi and anti joins avoid materializing right-side columns and can reduce duplication compared to `JOIN + DISTINCT`. DataFusion SQL docs explicitly support left/right semi and left/right anti joins. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text
Use SEMI for EXISTS.
Use ANTI for NOT EXISTS.
Avoid inner join + DISTINCT for existence logic.
Prefer semi/anti joins when only preserved-side columns are needed.
```

---

## 23.19 Lateral joins

### Correlated right relation

```sql
SELECT
  d.name,
  e.name
FROM departments AS d
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT name
  FROM employees
  WHERE employees.dept_id = d.id
) AS e ON true;
```

Lateral joins permit the right-hand relation to refer to columns from the left side. DataFusion docs require the `LATERAL` keyword and document `LEFT JOIN LATERAL` support. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text
Use LATERAL for correlated FROM subqueries.
Expect less optimization freedom than ordinary joins.
Avoid lateral joins for simple equijoins; use JOIN ON.
Test physical plan and row counts carefully.
```

---

## 23.20 Natural join warning

```sql
SELECT *
FROM x NATURAL JOIN y;
```

Natural join automatically chooses common column names as join keys; if there are no common columns, it behaves like a cross join. This is dangerous for generated SQL because schema changes can silently change join predicates. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text
Never generate NATURAL JOIN by default.
Use explicit JOIN ... ON.
If user requests natural join, snapshot common-column list before execution.
Validate output cardinality risk.
```

---

## 23.21 Join explain diagnostics

### Logical/physical explain

```sql
EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM fact AS f
JOIN dim AS d
  ON f.dim_id = d.id
WHERE d.category = 'active';
```

### Analyze

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT *
FROM fact AS f
JOIN dim AS d
  ON f.dim_id = d.id
WHERE d.category = 'active';
```

Inspect for:

```text
HashJoinExec vs SortMergeJoinExec vs NestedLoopJoinExec
RepartitionExec on join keys
FilterExec before join
ProjectionExec before join
build/probe side ordering
JoinFilter presence
Dynamic filter / scan filter behavior if visible
spills / memory / elapsed metrics in EXPLAIN ANALYZE
```

DataFusion’s `EXPLAIN` documentation distinguishes logical and physical plan output, and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes the query and reports operator metrics. ([Apache DataFusion][11])

---

## 23.22 Join tuning profiles

### Default analytics profile

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.repartition_joins = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
```

Use for equijoin-heavy bounded analytics with sufficient memory.

### Memory-limited profile

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = false;
SET datafusion.optimizer.repartition_joins = true;
```

Use when large build-side hash tables create memory pressure and sort-merge join is acceptable.

### Range-join experimental profile

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_piecewise_merge_join = true;
```

Use only when workloads contain single range predicates and benchmarks prove benefit. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

### Streaming join profile

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning = false;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
```

Use for unbounded/streaming sources where buffer pruning and bounded state are required.

---

## 23.23 Query-shape rewriting rules

### Bad: function-wrapped keys

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a
JOIN b
  ON lower(a.email) = lower(b.email);
```

Better if data can be normalized earlier:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a_norm AS a
JOIN b_norm AS b
  ON a.email_norm = b.email_norm;
```

### Bad: existence through join + distinct

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT c.*
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.id = o.customer_id;
```

Better:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM customers AS c
LEFT SEMI JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.id = o.customer_id;
```

### Bad: accidental cross join

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a, b;
```

Better:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a
JOIN b
  ON a.id = b.a_id;
```

Agent rules:

```text
Expose equality keys plainly.
Normalize join keys before join.
Prefer semi/anti for existence.
Avoid implicit comma joins.
Use explicit ON predicates.
```

---

## 23.24 Custom provider considerations for joins

If implementing a `TableProvider`, your metadata strongly affects join planning.

```text
Provide:
  accurate schema
  conservative statistics
  row count if known
  byte size if known
  sortedness if guaranteed
  partitioning if guaranteed
  filter pushdown capabilities
  projection pushdown
```

The optimizer uses statistics and physical properties to make choices such as join side, algorithm, repartitioning, and sort requirements; DataFusion physical join docs also rely on child ordering, partitioning, and memory behavior. ([Docs.rs][4])

Agent rules:

```text
Wrong stats can make the optimizer pick a bad build side.
False ordering metadata can remove necessary sorts.
False partitioning metadata can break distributed join correctness.
Unsupported filters should be Unsupported, not Exact.
```

---

## 23.25 Testing matrix

```text
[ ] inner equijoin result
[ ] left/right/full outer unmatched rows and nulls
[ ] semi/anti output schema and row count
[ ] NULL join-key behavior
[ ] duplicate key multiplicity
[ ] join filter correctness
[ ] non-equi join fallback/algorithm
[ ] piecewise merge range join if enabled
[ ] lateral join correlated semantics
[ ] natural join common-column detection if allowed
[ ] cross join row explosion safeguards
[ ] EXPLAIN operator selection
[ ] EXPLAIN ANALYZE metrics
[ ] memory-limited hash join behavior

[ ] streaming symmetric hash join bounded-state behavior
```

## 23.26 Deployment advisory

```text
Bounded analytics:
  prefer hash join by default.
  use repartition_joins for large parallel equijoins.
  provide stats for better build/probe selection.
  configure memory limit and spill path.

Memory-constrained workloads:
  consider prefer_hash_join=false.
  exploit sorted inputs.
  inspect SortMergeJoinExec plans.

Streaming/unbounded workloads:
  avoid unbounded cross/full joins.
  require time/range pruning.
  consider symmetric hash join with pruning.
  disable symmetric joins without pruning if unbounded buffers are unacceptable.

Generated SQL:
  never use NATURAL JOIN by default.
  never generate comma joins.
  use SEMI/ANTI for existence.
  qualify columns.
  alias duplicate output columns.
```

---

## 23.27 Anti-pattern inventory

* Natural join in generated SQL.
* Accidental comma/cross join.
* Joining two huge tables with no equality key and no range specialization.
* Function-wrapped join keys that block equijoin extraction.
* Wide `SELECT *` before joins.
* Build side larger than probe side in hash join.
* Relying on hash join in memory-limited settings without spill/resource planning.
* Enabling piecewise merge join globally without benchmark coverage.
* Unbounded symmetric hash join without pruning/window constraints.
* Treating join physical plan strings as stable across versions without pinning.
* Ignoring `NULL` join-key semantics.
* Using inner join + distinct for existence checks.
* Exposing lateral joins in generated SQL when simple equijoin suffices.
* False custom-source statistics leading to bad join choices.
* False ordering/partitioning metadata in custom providers.

---

```text
[ ] Choose join type: inner / left / right / full / semi / anti / cross / lateral.
[ ] Prefer explicit JOIN ... ON.
[ ] Avoid NATURAL JOIN unless user explicitly requests it.
[ ] Avoid CROSS JOIN unless Cartesian product is intended.
[ ] Use SEMI for EXISTS and ANTI for NOT EXISTS.
[ ] Keep equijoin keys syntactically visible.
[ ] Move single-table predicates to WHERE for pushdown.
[ ] Alias/qualify duplicate columns.
[ ] Inspect EXPLAIN for HashJoinExec / SortMergeJoinExec / NestedLoopJoinExec / PiecewiseMergeJoinExec / SymmetricHashJoinExec.
[ ] For hash join, ensure smaller side can be build side.
[ ] For memory pressure, consider sort-merge join and spill configuration.
[ ] For single range predicate, optionally test piecewise merge join.
[ ] For streaming, require pruning/window constraints before symmetric hash join.
[ ] Configure repartition_joins for large parallel equijoins.
[ ] Test NULL keys, duplicate keys, outer unmatched rows, and join filters.
[ ] Validate custom provider stats/ordering/partitioning before trusting join plans.
```
